help.title: Help
help.today.title: The day view
help.today.body:
Everything recorded for one day, with running timers at the top and both totals above the list.

Several timers may run at once, because work genuinely happens in parallel — a build running for one client while a meeting for another is under way. Overlapping entries are recorded exactly as they happened and never split between assignments automatically, because a split would be a guess that ends up on an invoice.

That is why two totals are shown. **Tracked** is the sum of every entry, and it is what gets billed. **Elapsed** is how much of the day was covered by at least one entry. When they differ, the difference is shown as **Overlap** — it is information, not an error.

Gaps between entries are marked as unaccounted time. They are prompts, never filled in for you.
help.quickadd.title: Quick add
help.quickadd.body:
One line becomes one entry:

`2h acme/migration fixed the login redirect #travel`

Read in order: a leading duration or time range, then an assignment, then any `#tags`, and whatever remains is the note.

Durations accept `1.5`, `1,5`, `1h30`, `90m` and `1:30`. A bare whole number means minutes, because `30` almost always means half an hour. A time range like `9:00-10:30` sets the start and end instead.

Assignment names are matched against what you have worked on recently, so a fragment is usually enough. If more than one matches, or nothing does, the full form opens pre-filled rather than the tool guessing — a wrong guess that silently becomes billable time is worse than a second click.
help.week.title: The week view
help.week.body:
A grid of assignments against days, which is the shape most timesheets are approved in.

Rows are ordered by customer and then by name, and stay in that order between weeks, so the grid can be read across time rather than reshuffling on every visit.

Cell values are decimal hours, the form invoicing systems expect. The day totals along the bottom are summed time, matching the **Tracked** figure rather than elapsed coverage.
help.entries.title: Entries and export
help.entries.body:
Every entry in a date range, filtered as you like. This is also what every export is generated from, so a download is exactly what is on screen.

The filter lives in the URL, so a filtered view can be bookmarked or sent to a colleague.

**CSV** is UTF-8 with a byte order mark, so Excel on Windows reads non-ASCII customer names correctly. **JSON** follows a documented, versioned schema and carries both the recorded and the billable duration along with the rounding rule that produced it, so a downstream system can verify the arithmetic rather than trust it.
help.admin.title: Customers, projects and assignments
help.admin.body:
Three levels: a **customer** is who gets billed, a **project** is a body of work for them, and an **assignment** is the thing a timer actually runs against — the granularity people describe their day in.

Colours and icons are not decoration. They are what makes the day view scannable at a glance, and the colour is stored as a palette name rather than a fixed value so it stays legible in all seven themes.

Nothing here is ever deleted, only archived. Deleting a customer would leave last year's invoice unable to say who was billed.

Rates resolve from the most specific level outwards: assignment, then the person's rate on the project, then the project, then the customer, then the instance default. The rate and the rounding rule are copied onto each entry when it is billed, so changing a rate tomorrow cannot alter what was invoiced today.
help.users.title: Users and access
help.users.body:
Four roles. An **admin** can do everything. A **manager** owns the customers and projects they are a member of, approves timesheets and sees money. A **member** records their own time and reads the projects they belong to. A **client** gets read-only reports for their own customer and nothing else.

The role is only half of it: **project membership** is what scopes what each person actually sees. A manager with no memberships sees nothing, which is deliberate — a new account starts with the least privilege and someone has to grant access explicitly.

Changing a role, disabling an account or changing a password signs that person out everywhere immediately. A privilege change that leaves old sessions running has not taken effect.
help.themes.title: Themes and accessibility
help.themes.body:
Seven themes: light, dark, gold, sand, spring, autumn and high contrast. The choice is stored against your account, so it follows you to another device.

The high-contrast theme meets WCAG 2.1 AA contrast ratios and is verified by an automated test, so a future change to the colours cannot quietly break it.

Every screen works without a mouse. Press the shortcut key shown in the footer for the full list. Colour is never the only carrier of meaning — status always has a label or an icon as well as a hue.

help.expenses.title: Expenses
help.expenses.body:
**Billable** and **reimbursable** are separate questions, and this application never conflates them.

A taxi you paid for and re-charge to the client is both. A hotel the client booked directly is neither. Your own train ticket on an internal project is reimbursable but not billable.

Because they are separate, reports total them separately: billable expenses join the invoice, reimbursable ones are money owed back to a person.

A markup percentage applies only to the billable side, and the billed amount is frozen when the expense is recorded — the same reasoning that freezes a rate onto a time entry.
help.inbox.title: Time proposed for you
help.inbox.body:
A colleague can record time in your name — useful when you worked together and one of you tracks time properly.

It does not become your time until you say so. Until you accept, the entry counts for nothing: not in your totals, not in a report, not on an invoice.

You can accept it, edit it and then accept, or reject it with a reason. A rejected proposal is kept rather than deleted, so the record of what was claimed survives the disagreement.
help.backup.title: Backup and restore
help.backup.body:
A backup is a single JSON file holding your customers, projects, assignments, time entries and expenses.

You can take the whole thing, or only part of it — one customer, one project, or one date range. A partial backup is a normal backup file; it simply contains less.

Restoring **merges**: a record that is already present is skipped rather than duplicated, so restoring the same file twice is harmless and restoring an old backup does not delete newer work.

Automatic backups are off unless enabled in the configuration file. Writing copies of your data on a schedule you did not ask for is your decision to make.

approvals.title: Approvals
approvals.intro: A submitted week is locked to the person who submitted it. Nobody decides on their own timesheet.
approvals.queue.empty: Nothing is waiting for a decision.
approvals.mine.empty: You have not submitted a week yet.
approvals.reopen.confirm: Reopen this approved week? The change is recorded.

help.approvals.title: Submitting and approving a week
help.approvals.body:
A week is the unit that gets declared finished. Submitting one says "these are my hours" and locks the week to you: time in it cannot be added, edited, moved or deleted while the lock holds.

A submission that has not been decided can be **withdrawn** by the person who made it - people remember something after they submit, and needing a manager to undo that makes them submit late instead.

Only a manager approves, and never their own week, whatever their role. A rejection needs a reason, because "rejected" on its own leaves the owner guessing and they will simply resubmit the same hours.

An approved week can be **reopened**. It is a deliberate act and it is recorded, which is better than the alternative: a system with no way back forces people to correct a mistake by inventing an adjustment somewhere else.
help.editing.title: Correcting an entry
help.editing.body:
The pencil on any row opens the entry for correction. The commonest mistake is a duration in the wrong unit - **8m** where **8h** was meant - so the duration is shown in the same notation it accepts, and the day and start time are shown beside it.

An end time, if you give one, is used instead of the duration. It is left empty on the form for that reason: a prefilled end time would silently overrule a duration you had just corrected.

Every change is recorded in the audit trail, including what the value was before, so a figure that has been corrected can still be explained later.

If the week has been submitted or approved, the entry cannot be changed until the week is withdrawn or reopened.
entry.kind.help: Overtime and travel are often billed differently. Which this was is your call - the customer's contract decides what each is worth.
rules.title: Contract terms — %s
rules.intro: Terms beyond the base hourly rate. Every field is optional: left empty, this customer bills exactly as it would without any of them.
rules.overtime.help: What an hour is worth once it is beyond the agreed working time.
rules.overtime.rate.help: An absolute rate. If set, it is used instead of the multiplier below.
rules.overtime.multiplier: Overtime as % of the base rate
rules.overtime.multiplier.help: 150 is time and a half, 200 is double time. Left empty, overtime bills at the ordinary rate.
rules.overtime.threshold.help: These only produce a reminder. Nothing is reclassified automatically: whether an hour counts as overtime is a contractual decision, not one this tool should make on your behalf.
rules.travel.help: Time spent travelling for this customer, recorded in full either way.
rules.travel.multiplier: Travel as % of the base rate
rules.travel.multiplier.help: 50 bills travel at half the ordinary rate. Used when no absolute travel rate is set.
rules.reimbursement.help: What gets paid back, at what markup, and against what evidence.
rules.expense.markup.help: Added to the billable side only. The reimbursed amount is always the cost.
rules.mileage.help: Set this and a distance can be claimed directly, priced without anyone doing the multiplication by hand.
rules.receipt.help: A week cannot be submitted while an expense above this amount has no receipt attached.
overtime.notice.week: Week of %s: %s recorded for %s, %s past the agreed %s.
overtime.notice.help: Mark the hours that were overtime, or leave them as work if that is what was agreed. Nothing is reclassified for you.
expense.quantity.help: Priced at the customer's mileage rate or per diem. Leave the amount empty and it is calculated.
expense.receipt.needed.title: This customer requires a receipt above a set amount. The week cannot be submitted until one is attached.
